Article.ArticleTitle: Severe headache as a key symptom in bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia-induced primary hyperaldosteronism: A case report.

Abstract.AbstractText: Severe headaches can have various causes, but they are commonly associated with common conditions such as tension-type headaches or migraines. However, in cases where these common causes do not explain the symptoms, it becomes essential to investigate secondary causes. This case highlights the importance of considering rare conditions, such as bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia-induced primary hyperaldosteronism, as a potential cause of persistent headaches and refractory hypertension. The study aims to explore the relationship between primary hyperaldosteronism and severe headaches, emphasizing the importance of early diagnosis and appropriate treatment for improving patient outcomes.
A 25-year-old male presented with severe, sporadic occipital headaches that had been ongoing for 2 months.

Initial tests, including a complete blood count, thyroid-stimulating hormone levels, and echocardiography were normal. Despite antihypertensive treatment, his blood pressure remained elevated. Further investigations revealed a high aldosterone-to-renin ratio, indicative of primary hyperaldosteronism. Imaging confirmed the diagnosis of bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia.

Management of bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia involves medical therapy with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like spironolactone or eplerenone. These medications block the effects of aldosterone, helping to control blood pressure and correct electrolyte imbalances.

The patient's refractory hypertension to initial therapies underscores the necessity of considering secondary causes of hypertension early in the diagnostic process, particularly in young patients without a significant family history of hypertension.

This case highlights the importance of considering secondary causes of hypertension and severe headaches when common treatments do not yield the expected results. Timely diagnosis of conditions like primary hyperaldosteronism can significantly improve patient outcomes through targeted therapy.

Article.ArticleTitle: COVID-19 Vaccination and the Risk of Migraine Chronification: A Comparative Cohort Study of Vaccinated and Unvaccinated Patients With Episodic Migraine.

Abstract.AbstractText: Headache is among the most frequently reported adverse events after COVID-19 vaccination, and patients with migraine often fear that vaccination will worsen their disease or accelerate the transition from episodic to chronic migraine. Controlled data comparing vaccinated and unvaccinated patients with migraine are scarce.

We conducted a comparative prospective cohort study of 60 adults with pre-existing episodic migraine, classified at enrolment as vaccinated (n = 30) or unvaccinated (n = 30) against COVID-19, at a single neuroscience clinic in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and followed for 6 months. Migraine status (episodic or chronic, per ICHD-3) was assessed at 3 and 6 months. Between-group chronification was compared using Fisher's exact test with odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs); patient-level transitions were also examined. No a priori sample-size calculation was performed.

There were no statistically significant baseline differences between groups in age (30.3 ± 5.07 vs. 30.5 ± 4.46 years; p = 0.87), sex (p = 0.78), or preventive medication (p = 0.58). Provisional chronic-frequency status was recorded in 5/30 vaccinated versus 11/30 unvaccinated patients at 3 months (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.10-1.16; p = 0.14), and chronic migraine in 3/30 versus 6/30 at 6 months (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.10-1.97; p = 0.47). All such transitions occurred by 3 months, with no new cases between 3 and 6 months; the confidence intervals were wide and included no difference.

In this small observational cohort, no statistically significant association was detected between COVID-19 vaccination and migraine chronification. The wide confidence intervals preclude firm conclusions regarding either harm or benefit, and larger, adequately powered studies are needed.
